catalog_citation: Revithiadou, Anthi (1999). Headmost Accent Wins: Head Dominance and Ideal Prosodic Form in Lexical Accent Systems. PhD dissertation, Leiden (HIL/LOT Dissertations 15). Chapter 3 'Lexical Accents and Prosodic Form', open copy ROA-388.
catalog_quote: Greek syllable structure lacks distinctions of phonological weight; all syllables are of equal phonological weight (Joseph and Philippaki 1987). Greek is a bounded system; the scope of primary stress is limited to the last three syllables of the word. Feet in Greek are trochaic. ... Morphologically equivalent words such as án7ropos 'man', fantáros 'soldier' and uranós 'sky', for instance, exhibit phonologically unmotivated differences in stress. The complexity of the system is further enhanced by accentual alternations that take place within the paradigm as in án7ropos (NOM.sg), an7rópu (GEN.sg). ... the best way to analyze stress in nouns and adjectives is to assume that the respective morphemes are inherently marked. Lexical accents mark one of the last three positions of the word because Greek is a three-syllable-window language. For example, stress is on the antepenult in án7ropos, …
sweep_summary: Modern Greek (mode1248) is in the catalog as LEXICAL on Revithiadou 1999 (ROA-388). Of 38 title hits, 16 are Ancient Greek or metrics (Allen, Probert, Devine & Stephens, Hirt, Bubenik, Galton, Hoenigswald x2, Pulgram, Steriade x2, Grundt, Miller, Nagy, Schulze 1711) and 12 are intonation/sentence prosody or off-topic (Arvaniti x3, Baltazani x2, Georgakopoulos & Skopeteas, Georgiafentis & Sfakianaki, Condoravdi et al., Malikouti-Drachman & Drachman 1981, Yoo, Archakis, Kotsifas, Agouraki). Word-stress items: van Oostendorp 2012 (open preprint fetched sources and read: lexical stress, three-syllable window, antepenult default, past-tense verbs uniformly antepenultimate; CONFIRMS the catalog, does not supersede Revithiadou), Dieterich 1904 (IF 16, public-domain scan fetched sources from archive.org; accent retraction as a derivational device, consistent with lexical coding), and three unread paywalled/print items: Drachman & Malikouti-Drachman 1999 Eurotyp chapter (high priority, DOI 10.1515/9783110197082.2.897), Botinis 1989 Lund monograph (high, print only, Libris 7677465), Kaisse 1982 Linguistics (medium, DOI 10.1515/ling.1982.20.1-2.59), Nespor & Ralli 1994 compounds (medium). Peperkamp 1996 and Kaisse 1976 unresolved (low).fr, lingbuzz and archive.org.

new_statements.quote: There is consensus that stress is lexical in Greek, in the sense that it is largely unpredictable by phonological criteria such as syllable weight or vowel quality, and dependent on lexical specification instead. ... There is one important observation on the lexical assignment of stress, in all categories of Greek words: it is restricted by a three-syllable window (at least in the standard language, which is discussed here). Stress can fall on any of the last three syllables, but not on any other syllable of the word.

new_statements.locator: preprint §2 'Lexical stress in Greek' and §2.1 'The phonology of nominal stress', pp. 3-4
new_statements.reading: Lexical (unpredictable) stress within a right-edge three-syllable window; antepenultimate stress is the default (stress shift under inflection, compound stress, and the whole verbal past tense: 'Virtually all past tense forms of the Greek verb are characterised by antepenultimate stress'); enclisis adds a second stress on the last two syllables. Confirms the catalog's 'lexical' coding and its window/default notes; adds that past-tense verb stress is morphologically fixed on the antepenult.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation, the domain quote and the window-exception quote is present verbatim in the held ROA-388 ch.3 text at the stated pages (85-86, 88, 98). The deciding source is a specialist 1999 dissertation on lexical accent systems with Greek as its central case, openly held, and two further held descriptions (Joseph 2006 ELL2; Joseph & Tserdanelis 2003) state the same facts: stress confined to the last three syllables, position lexically/morphologically determined, no weight sensitivity. sources.quote: There is consensus that stress is lexical in Greek, in the sense that it is largely unpredictable by phonological criteria such as syllable weight or vowel quality, and dependent on lexical specification instead. ... There is one important observation on the lexical assignment of stress, in all categories of Greek words: it is restricted by a three-syllable window (at least in the standard language, which is discussed here). Stress can fall on any of the last three syllables, but not on any other syllable of the word.
sources.locator: preprint (19 May 2012) §2 'Lexical stress in Greek' and §2.1 'The phonology of nominal stress', pp. 3-4; abstract p. 1
sources.note: Stress is lexical (unpredictable from weight), confined to a three-syllable window; enclisis adds a stress on the last two syllables (GónDolá-mu); inflection-driven shift keeps stress in the window (máTima ~ maTímatos); antepenultimate stress acts as default (compounds kuzinomáxero) and 'virtually all past tense forms of the Greek verb are characterised by antepenultimate stress' (abstract), analysed as a floating-foot proclitic. Fully consistent with the catalog's 'lexical' coding and its window/default notes; adds the verbal past-tense generalisation.

sources.citation: Dieterich, K. (1904). Akzent- und Bedeutungsverschiebung im Mittel- und Neugriechischen. Indogermanische Forschungen 16: 1-26.
sources.quote: Die Tonverschiebung vollzieht sich im Alt- und Neugriechischen tatsächlich nach dem gleichen Gesetz: das ursprüngliche Wort wird auf der letzten, das abgeleitete auf der vorletzten Silbe betont. Und wie im Altgriechischen, so ist auch im Neugriechischen mit dieser Verschiebung des Tons nicht nur eine solche der Bedeutung, sondern sogar eine solche der Funktion verbunden. [The accent shift proceeds in Ancient and Modern Greek by the same law: the base word is stressed on the final, the derived word on the penultimate syllable; and in Modern Greek as in Ancient Greek this shift of accent is tied not only to a shift of meaning but even of function.]
sources.note: Historical-derivational study: accent retraction (oxytone base > paroxytone derivative, e.g. kontós 'short' > Kóntos name; adverbs from prepositions) is a productive lexical/morphological device in Medieval and Modern Greek, so accent position is contrastive and word-specific. Consistent with the 'lexical' coding; silent on the three-syllable window and default.
